title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
17.2 Introduction to Diffusion Models
Denoising diffusion models consist of two processes:

Forward diffusion process (fixed): gradually adds Gaussian noise to input data, transforming an image into pure noise.
Reverse denoising process (learned): learns to generate data from noise by iteratively denoising, using a neural network.







TipRemark: Key References




Sohl-Dickstein et al., Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics, ICML 2015
Ho et al., Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM), NeurIPS 2020
Song et al., Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations, ICLR 2021









Figure 17.1: The diffusion model framework: the forward process gradually adds noise to data, while the learned reverse process denoises to generate new samples.



The central design questions are:

How to design the forward process? In particular, how to choose the noise schedule?
How to design the reverse process? What is the optimization objective for training the neural network \mu_\theta, and what architecture to use?

title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
17.3 Forward Diffusion Process
Starting from a data point x_0 \sim P_{\text{data}}, we construct a sequence x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_T by adding i.i.d. Gaussian noise at each step:
x_t = \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t}\, \varepsilon_{t-1}, \qquad \varepsilon_t \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0, I_d).
Equivalently, the conditional density of x_t given x_{t-1} is:
q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_t;\; \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\, x_{t-1},\; \beta_t\, I\right).
The joint distribution over the entire forward chain factorizes as a Markov chain:
q(x_{1:T} \mid x_0) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}).

17.3.1 Noise Schedule
The noise schedule \{\beta_t\}_{t=1}^{T} controls how quickly information is destroyed:

\beta_t is close to 0 when t is small (gentle noise at the start).
\beta_t grows over time so that x_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) by the end.
In practice (DDPM): \beta_1 = \beta_{\min} \approx 10^{-3}, \beta_T = \beta_{\max} \approx 0.02, with linear interpolation between them. The number of steps T is typically 1000.


  
  Figure 11.1: Linear noise schedule β_t and cumulative signal retention ᾱ_t = ∏(1−β_i). As t grows, ᾱ_t → 0 and the signal vanishes.



17.3.2 Why \sqrt{1-\beta_t} and \sqrt{\beta_t}?

Theorem 17.1 (Theorem 11.1 (Variance Preservation)) For any a, b \in \mathbb{R}, define the recursion X_t = a\, X_{t-1} + b\, \varepsilon_{t-1}. If we want X_T \to \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) in distribution as T \to \infty, then we need
a = \sqrt{1-\beta}, \qquad b = \sqrt{\beta} \qquad \text{for some } \beta \in (0, 1].

This result explains why the diffusion coefficients take the specific form \sqrt{1-\beta_t} and \sqrt{\beta_t}: they are the unique choice (up to parameterization) that preserves unit variance across the recursion, ensuring the process converges to standard Gaussian noise regardless of the starting distribution.

Proof. By unrolling the recursion:
X_t = a^t X_0 + b\left(\varepsilon_{t-1} + a\,\varepsilon_{t-2} + \cdots + a^{t-1}\varepsilon_0\right).
The variance of the noise term is:
\operatorname{Var}(\text{noise}) = b^2 (1 + a^2 + a^4 + \cdots + a^{2(t-1)}) I = b^2 \cdot \frac{1 - a^{2t}}{1 - a^2}\, I.
For convergence to \mathcal{N}(0, I), we need two conditions: (1) the signal component a^t X_0 must vanish, which requires |a| < 1; and (2) as t \to \infty, the noise variance must tend to I, giving \frac{b^2}{1 - a^2} = 1, hence a^2 + b^2 = 1. Setting a = \sqrt{1-\beta} and b = \sqrt{\beta} satisfies both conditions. This completes the proof. \blacksquare







TipRemark: Trigonometric Analogy



The condition a^2 + b^2 = 1 is analogous to \sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1. Writing v = \cos\theta \cdot x + \sin\theta \cdot y with \operatorname{Var}(x) = 1 preserves variance: \operatorname{Var}(v) = 1. The diffusion coefficients \sqrt{1-\beta_t} and \sqrt{\beta_t} play exactly this role.




17.3.3 Closed-Form Distribution: q(x_t \mid x_0)
A key advantage of the Gaussian forward process is that we can compute the marginal distribution of x_t given x_0 in closed form, without iterating through all intermediate steps.

Definition 17.1 (Definition 11.1 (Cumulative Noise Parameters)) Let \alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t and define the cumulative product:
\bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{i=1}^{t} \alpha_i = \prod_{i=1}^{t} (1 - \beta_i).

The parameter \bar{\alpha}_t measures how much of the original signal survives after t steps of noise addition. When \bar{\alpha}_t \approx 1, the data point x_0 is mostly preserved; when \bar{\alpha}_t \approx 0, the signal has been almost entirely replaced by noise.

Theorem 17.2 (Theorem 11.2 (Marginal Distribution of Forward Process)) The conditional distribution of x_t given x_0 is:
q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(x_t;\; \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0,\; (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t)\, I_d\right).
Equivalently, we can sample x_t directly as:
x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\, \varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d).

This is a crucial result for practical implementation: it allows us to sample x_t at any arbitrary timestep t directly from x_0 without simulating the entire Markov chain step by step. This makes training efficient, since we can randomly sample a timestep t and immediately compute the noisy input x_t for the loss function.

Proof. We derive this by recursive substitution. Starting from x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\, x_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\, \varepsilon_{t-1}:
x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}}\, x_{t-2} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\, \varepsilon_{t-1} + \sqrt{\alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1})}\, \varepsilon_{t-2}.
Since \varepsilon_{t-1} and \varepsilon_{t-2} are independent standard Gaussians, the sum of the two independent Gaussian noise terms has variance (1-\alpha_t) + \alpha_t(1-\alpha_{t-1}) = 1 - \alpha_t \alpha_{t-1}. So we can write:
w_{t-2} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, (1 - \alpha_t\alpha_{t-1})\, I).
Applying this merging of Gaussian noise terms recursively down to x_0, we accumulate the product \bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{i=1}^t \alpha_i as the signal coefficient and 1 - \bar{\alpha}_t as the total noise variance. Hence we conclude the proof. \blacksquare







Summary of the Forward Process:
x_t \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0,\; (1-\bar\alpha_t)\, I\right).
As t \to T, \bar\alpha_t \to 0, so x_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I) — pure noise.




  
  Figure 11.2: The forward diffusion process in 1D. A data point x_0 is gradually corrupted: the signal coefficient √ᾱ_t shrinks while the noise variance 1−ᾱ_t grows.

title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
17.4 Reverse Denoising Process
The reverse process starts from pure noise \widetilde{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d) and iteratively denoises using a learned neural network. The joint distribution of the reverse chain is:
p_\theta(\widetilde{x}_{0:T}) = p(\widetilde{x}_T) \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_\theta(\widetilde{x}_{t-1} \mid \widetilde{x}_t),
where:

p(\widetilde{x}_T) = \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{x}_T; 0, I_d) is the starting distribution (pure noise).
Each reverse step is parameterized as a Gaussian:

p_\theta(\widetilde{x}_{t-1} \mid \widetilde{x}_t) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\widetilde{x}_{t-1};\; \mu_\theta(\widetilde{x}_t, t),\; \sigma_t^2\, I\right).
Here \mu_\theta(\cdot, \cdot) is a trainable neural network (typically a U-Net / denoising autoencoder) that takes the current noisy image \widetilde{x}_t and timestep t as input, and predicts the denoised mean.

17.4.1 Generating an Image






ImportantAlgorithm: Image Generation Procedure



Once the network \mu_\theta is trained and the variance schedule \{\sigma_t^2\}_{t=1}^T is fixed:

Sample \widetilde{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I_d).
For t = T, T-1, \ldots, 1: sample \widetilde{x}_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_\theta(\widetilde{x}_t, t),\; \sigma_t^2 I\right).
Output \widetilde{x}_0.

Goal: The distribution of \widetilde{x}_0 should match P_{\text{data}}, so the generated images look realistic.








TipRemark: Mental Picture



The forward process maps data x_0 \sim P_{\text{data}} through a chain x_0 \to x_1 \to \cdots \to x_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I). The reverse process runs backwards: \widetilde{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I) \to \widetilde{x}_{T-1} \to \cdots \to \widetilde{x}_0. When T is sufficiently large, the forward endpoint x_T and the reverse starting point \widetilde{x}_T have nearly the same distribution \mathcal{N}(0, I). If the reverse transitions closely match the true posterior q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t), then \widetilde{x}_0 will be distributed like real data.

title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
17.5 Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO)
The key question is: how do we train \mu_\theta? There are two major approaches:

Derive the continuous-time limit (stochastic differential equation) and then the Reverse SDE.
View the forward and reverse processes as two joint distributions over (x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_T) and minimize their divergence. This leads to the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO).

We focus on the ELBO approach.

17.5.1 ELBO for a Simplified Model
Consider a simplified setting with just one latent variable z (i.e., T=1):

x \sim f_0(\cdot): signal with unknown parameters.
q(z \mid x): a noisy channel that generates observation z from signal x.
p(z): a noise distribution, e.g., \mathcal{N}(0, I).
p_\theta(x \mid z): a neural-network-based denoising method.

The marginal likelihood under our model is:
p_\theta(x) = \int p(z)\, p_\theta(x \mid z)\, dz.
We want to maximize \sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i) (MLE). But the integral makes direct optimization hard.

Theorem 17.3 (Theorem 11.3 (Evidence Lower Bound)) For any conditional distribution q(z \mid x) (called the variational distribution) and for all x:
\log p_\theta(x) \geq \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q(\cdot \mid x)}\!\left[\log p_\theta(x, z) - \log q(z \mid x)\right] = \text{ELBO}(\theta).

The ELBO provides a tractable lower bound on the log-likelihood, which is typically intractable to compute directly due to the integral over latent variables. By maximizing this lower bound instead of the true log-likelihood, we obtain a principled training objective. The tighter the bound (i.e., the smaller the KL gap), the closer the ELBO is to the true objective.


17.5.2 Proof of the ELBO

Proof. Note that p_\theta(x) = \int p_\theta(x, z)\, dz and p_\theta(x, z) = p(z) \cdot p_\theta(x \mid z). Also, for any distribution q(z \mid x), we have \int q(z \mid x)\, dz = 1. Thus:
\log p_\theta(x) = \log p_\theta(x) \cdot \int q(z \mid x)\, dz = \int q(z \mid x) \cdot \log p_\theta(x)\, dz. \quad \text{(1)}
Using p_\theta(x, z) = p_\theta(x) \cdot p_\theta(z \mid x), we write:
\log p_\theta(x) = \log p_\theta(x, z) - \log p_\theta(z \mid x). \quad \text{(2)}
Substituting (2) into (1) and separating the terms involving q(z \mid x):
\log p_\theta(x) = \int q(z \mid x) \log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z \mid x)}\, dz \;+\; \int q(z \mid x) \log \frac{q(z \mid x)}{p_\theta(z \mid x)}\, dz.
The first term is the ELBO. The second term is D_{\text{KL}}(q(z \mid x) \,\|\, p_\theta(z \mid x)) \geq 0. Since \log p_\theta(x) = \text{ELBO} + \text{KL} \geq \text{ELBO}, we conclude the proof. \blacksquare







TipRemark



The ELBO holds for all choices of q(\cdot \mid x). Ideally, we want q(z \mid x) \approx p_\theta(z \mid x) so that the KL gap is small and the ELBO is tight. When the KL term is small, maximizing the ELBO is nearly equivalent to maximizing the log-likelihood.
Alternative proof via Jensen’s inequality (using Jensen’s inequality from convex function theory — see Part 3): Since \log is concave, \mathbb{E}[f(Z)] \leq f(\mathbb{E}[Z]), giving directly:
\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z \mid x)} q(z \mid x)\, dz \geq \mathbb{E}_{z \sim q(\cdot \mid x)}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x, z)}{q(z \mid x)}\right].




17.5.3 ELBO for Diffusion Models
Now we apply the ELBO framework to the full diffusion model with T steps. We have two processes:

Definition 17.2 (Definition 11.2 (Forward and Reverse Joint Distributions)) Forward process (fixed, acts as variational distribution):
q(\{x_t\}_{t=0}^T) = P_{\text{data}}(x_0) \prod_{t=1}^{T} q_t(x_t \mid x_{t-1}), \quad q_t(x' \mid x) = \mathcal{N}(x';\, \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\, x,\, \beta_t I).
Reverse process (learned, parameterized by \theta):
p_\theta(\{\widetilde{x}_t\}_{t=1}^T) = p(\widetilde{x}_T) \prod_{t=1}^{T} p_\theta(\widetilde{x}_{t-1} \mid \widetilde{x}_t), \quad p(\widetilde{x}_T) = \mathcal{N}(\widetilde{x}_T; 0, I_d).
Each p_\theta(\widetilde{x}_{t-1} \mid \widetilde{x}_t) is a neural-network-based conditional Gaussian distribution.

The forward process serves as the “variational distribution” in the ELBO framework: it defines how latent variables (x_1, \ldots, x_T) are generated from data x_0. The reverse process is the generative model we wish to train. The goal is to make the learned reverse transitions match the true posterior of the forward process as closely as possible.
The training objective is to maximize the ELBO, which decomposes into:
\text{ELBO}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x_{0:T})}{q(x_{1:T} \mid x_0)}\right].
After careful algebraic manipulation, the diffusion ELBO breaks into three types of terms:






Decomposition of the Diffusion ELBO:

Reconstruction term: \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x_0 \mid x_1)] — how well the model reconstructs data from the first latent.
Prior matching term: -D_{\text{KL}}(q(x_T \mid x_0) \,\|\, p(x_T)) — forward endpoint should match \mathcal{N}(0, I).
Denoising matching terms: -\sum_{t=2}^{T} \mathbb{E}_q\!\left[D_{\text{KL}}(q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0) \,\|\, p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t))\right] — the learned reverse step should match the true posterior at each timestep.

title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
17.6 Training Objective and Noise Prediction
The dominant terms in the ELBO are the denoising matching KL divergences. Since both q(x_{t-1} \mid x_t, x_0) and p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t) are Gaussian, the KL divergence reduces to comparing their means (the variances can be set to match).
Ho et al. (2020) showed that instead of predicting the mean \mu_\theta(x_t, t) directly, it is more effective to predict the noise. The reparameterization is:
\mu_\theta(x_t, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\!\left(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\, \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\right),
where \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) is a neural network that predicts the noise \varepsilon that was added. The simplified training loss becomes:






DDPM Simplified Loss:
\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \varepsilon}\!\left[\left\|\varepsilon - \epsilon_\theta\!\left(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\, \varepsilon,\; t\right)\right\|^2\right],
where t \sim \text{Uniform}(\{1, \ldots, T\}), x_0 \sim P_{\text{data}}, and \varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I).









TipRemark: Why Noise Prediction Works



Since x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\, \varepsilon, predicting the noise \varepsilon is equivalent to predicting x_0. Empirically, training the network to predict \varepsilon leads to better sample quality than directly predicting x_0 or \mu. This is because the noise prediction objective gives equal weight to all noise levels.



17.6.1 DDPM Training Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm: DDPM Training



repeat
    // Sample a data point and random timestep
    x_0 ~ P_data
    t ~ Uniform({1, ..., T})
    epsilon ~ N(0, I)
    // Compute noisy sample and take gradient step
    x_t <- sqrt(alpha_bar_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t) * epsilon
    Take gradient step on grad_theta ||epsilon - epsilon_theta(x_t, t)||^2
until converged




17.6.2 DDPM Sampling Algorithm






ImportantAlgorithm: DDPM Sampling



// Start from pure noise
x_T ~ N(0, I)
for t = T, T-1, ..., 1 do
    z ~ N(0, I) if t > 1, else z = 0
    x_{t-1} = (1/sqrt(alpha_t)) * (x_t - (beta_t/sqrt(1 - alpha_bar_t)) * epsilon_theta(x_t, t)) + sigma_t * z
end for
return x_0



  
  Figure 11.3: Score function ∇_x log q(x_t) for a Gaussian mixture at different noise levels. At high noise (large t), the score field is smooth and points toward the global center. At low noise (small t), it resolves individual modes.

title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
17.7 Interactive Demo
The following code demonstrates the forward diffusion process on a 1D Gaussian mixture. You can modify the noise schedule and number of steps to see how the data distribution transforms into pure noise.
#| eval: false
import numpy as np

# Parameters
T = 50            # number of diffusion steps
n_samples = 5000  # number of data points
beta_min, beta_max = 1e-3, 0.02

# Linear noise schedule
betas = np.linspace(beta_min, beta_max, T)
alphas = 1.0 - betas
alpha_bar = np.cumprod(alphas)

# Sample from a Gaussian mixture (3 modes)
np.random.seed(42)
modes = [-3.0, 0.0, 4.0]
weights = [0.3, 0.4, 0.3]
x0 = np.zeros(n_samples)
for i in range(n_samples):
    k = np.random.choice(len(modes), p=weights)
    x0[i] = modes[k] + 0.5 * np.random.randn()

# Forward diffusion at selected timesteps
steps_to_show = [0, 5, 15, 30, 49]
print("Forward Diffusion Process (1D Gaussian Mixture)")
print("=" * 50)
for t_idx in steps_to_show:
    if t_idx == 0:
        xt = x0.copy()
    else:
        eps = np.random.randn(n_samples)
        xt = np.sqrt(alpha_bar[t_idx]) * x0 + np.sqrt(1 - alpha_bar[t_idx]) * eps
    mean_val = np.mean(xt)
    std_val = np.std(xt)
    print(f"t={t_idx:3d}  alpha_bar={alpha_bar[min(t_idx, T-1)]:.4f}"
          f"  mean={mean_val:+.3f}  std={std_val:.3f}")

print()
print(f"At t={T-1}: alpha_bar = {alpha_bar[-1]:.6f}")
print(f"Signal nearly destroyed: sqrt(alpha_bar) = {np.sqrt(alpha_bar[-1]):.4f}")
print(f"Noise dominates: sqrt(1-alpha_bar) = {np.sqrt(1-alpha_bar[-1]):.4f}")






TipRemark: Looking Ahead



In the final lecture, we study the transformer architecture—attention mechanisms, positional encoding, and how optimization principles underpin training modern large language models.

title: 17  Diffusion Models
text:
Summary

Forward diffusion process. Starting from data x_0 \sim q(x_0), the forward process adds Gaussian noise over T steps via q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(x_t;\, \sqrt{1-\beta_t}\, x_{t-1},\, \beta_t I); the closed-form marginal is q(x_t | x_0) = \mathcal{N}(x_t;\, \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0,\, (1-\bar\alpha_t)I) where \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s=1}^{t}(1-\beta_s).
Reverse process and denoising. The generative model learns a reverse Markov chain p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t) that removes noise step-by-step; the neural network \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) predicts the noise added at each step.
ELBO and training objective. The variational lower bound decomposes into per-step KL divergences; the simplified DDPM loss reduces to \mathbb{E}_{t, x_0, \epsilon}\bigl[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\, \epsilon,\, t)\|^2\bigr]—a denoising score-matching objective.
Score matching connection. The score function \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t) points toward higher-density regions; the denoising network implicitly estimates this score, linking diffusion models to score-based generative modeling.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.1 What Will Be Covered
Adapted from slides by Anna Goldie (Stanford CS 224n), John Hewitt, and Song Han (MIT 6.5940)
The transformer architecture has fundamentally reshaped artificial intelligence. Since the publication of “Attention Is All You Need” in 2017, transformers have become the universal backbone for language models (GPT, Claude, LLaMA), vision models (ViT), protein structure prediction (AlphaFold), and much more. Understanding how transformers work is now essential for anyone working at the intersection of optimization and machine learning.
At its core, the transformer is built from a small set of mathematical operations — matrix multiplications, softmax normalization, and elementwise nonlinearities — all of which are trained end-to-end using the gradient-based optimization methods developed earlier in this course. The key innovation is the attention mechanism, which allows each token in a sequence to dynamically attend to every other token, computing a weighted average that captures long-range dependencies. Combined with positional encodings, residual connections, and layer normalization, these attention layers are stacked into deep networks with billions of parameters.
This chapter walks through the transformer architecture from the ground up. We will see how token embeddings map discrete words into continuous vectors, how self-attention computes context-dependent representations, and how the full decoder architecture generates text one token at a time. We also analyze the parameter count of GPT-3 to build concrete intuition for the scale of these models.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.2 1. Motivation
Transformer models are revolutionary. The foundational paper “Attention Is All You Need” (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the Transformer architecture, which has since become the backbone of virtually all modern AI systems: ChatGPT/GPT-4 (OpenAI), Claude (Anthropic), Gemini (Google), LLaMA (Meta), and many more.
Today, Transformer-based models dominate the LMSYS Chatbot Arena Leaderboard (Chiang et al., 2024), with models like GPT-4-Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, and Gemini 1.5 Pro at the top.
Transformers have even shown great promise outside of NLP:

Protein folding: AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) uses attention mechanisms
Image classification: Vision Transformer (ViT) outperforms ResNet-based baselines (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020)
ML for Systems: Transformer-based compiler models (GO-one) speed up other Transformer models (Zhou et al., 2020)


18.2.1 Language Tasks

Definition 18.1 (Two Main Types of Language Tasks) 1. Generative tasks (conditional generation): e.g., translation, code generation. \mathbb{P}(\text{text} \mid \text{text / image}).
2. Discriminative tasks (classification): e.g., part-of-speech classification, sentiment analysis. \mathbb{P}(\text{label} \mid \text{text}).

Understanding this distinction between generative and discriminative tasks is important because it directly determines which type of transformer architecture is appropriate: encoder-only models excel at discriminative tasks, while decoder-only models are designed for generation.

title: 18  Transformers
section: 18.3 2. Three Types of Transformer-Based Language Models
text:
18.3 2. Three Types of Transformer-Based Language Models
Depending on the task, transformers come in three flavors that differ in how information flows through the model. The choice between them determines whether the model can “see the whole input at once” (useful for classification) or must generate output one token at a time (necessary for text generation). Understanding these three variants clarifies why modern large language models are almost exclusively decoder-only.

18.3.1 Task Type 1: Encoder-Only (Feature Extraction + Discriminative Tasks)

Definition 18.2 (Encoder-Only Transformer) An encoder-only transformer creates a sequence of token-level features of the input (for discriminative tasks).

Input: sequence of tokens w_1, \ldots, w_L; L = sequence length
Output: sequence of features z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_L \in \mathbb{R}^d

Key characteristic: each z_\ell depends on the whole input. That is, z_\ell depends on \{w_1, \ldots, w_L\} for all \ell \in [L].
Extract global features for downstream tasks (trained separately using these features):

Token-level: part-of-speech classification
Sentence-level: sentiment analysis

Key examples: BERT, Vision Transformer (ViT)



18.3.2 Task Type 2: Decoder-Only (Autoregressive Generation)

Definition 18.3 (Decoder-Only Transformer) A decoder-only transformer generates a sequence of features for generating the next token.

Input: sequence of tokens w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_L
Output: sequence of features z_1, z_2, \ldots, z_L

Key characteristics:

Each z_\ell only depends on w_1, w_2, \ldots, w_\ell (autoregressive / cannot look into the future)
Predict w_{\ell+1} using z_\ell only, via a softmax prediction layer

Key examples: GPT family, LLaMA, Mistral


Example 18.1 (Autoregressive Generation) We want a model that predicts the next word given context. For “I am a Yale ?”, we want: \mathbb{P}(w_5 \mid w_{1:4}) = \mathbb{P}(\text{"student"} \mid \text{"I am a Yale"}).
An autoregressive LLM = Decoder-only TF + Prediction Head: \mathbb{P}_\theta(w_{\ell+1} \mid w_1, \ldots, w_\ell).
Autoregressive generation proceeds step by step:

\mathbb{P}(\text{"I"} \mid \text{prompt} = \text{"My name is X."})
\mathbb{P}(\text{"am"} \mid \text{prompt} = \text{"My name is X. I"})
\mathbb{P}(\text{"a"} \mid \text{prompt} = \text{"My name is X. I am"})
\mathbb{P}(\text{"Yale"} \mid \text{prompt} = \text{"My name is X. I am a"})
\mathbb{P}(\text{"student"} \mid \text{prompt} = \text{"My name is X. I am a Yale"})

Each output word is copied back into the input for the next prediction.



18.3.3 Task Type 3: Encoder-Decoder Transformer

Definition 18.4 (Encoder-Decoder Transformer) The original Transformer model (Vaswani et al., 2017). Used for machine translation and conditional generation.
The encoder processes the input sequence into features; the decoder autoregressively generates the output, attending to the encoder features via cross attention.
Example: (“Hello”, “world”, “!”) \to Encoder \to features \to Decoder \to (“Bonjour”, “le”, “monde”, “!”)







TipRemark: Current Landscape



Encoder-decoder models and encoder-only LLMs are not popular now.

Decoder-only models are most popular — GPT family, LLaMA, Mistral
Decoder-only models can also perform discriminative tasks
Only exception: Vision Transformer (ViT), which is encoder-only

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.4 3. Architectures of Transformers
Note: This is the most important part of this class, and it is very complicated.
There are many components of these neural networks. To introduce the architecture, we equivalently introduce the “forward” function: How is the input language token sequence transformed into the output?






Mental Picture (using GPT-3 as reference):

V = vocabulary size = 50,257
d = model dimension = 12,288
L = sequence length = 2,048

Input: w_1, \ldots, w_L (tokens, w_i \in \mathbb{R}^V one-hot). Transformer (embedding, MLP, attention, layer norm, residual link) produces features z_1, \ldots, z_L \in \mathbb{R}^d. Then a prediction layer produces the loss \ell_1, \ldots, \ell_L.




18.4.1 Prediction Head & Softmax
The prediction head is designed according to the task, which determines the loss function. A transformer outputs a real-valued vector z_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^d at each position, but for next-token prediction we need a probability distribution over the vocabulary. The softmax function bridges this gap by converting an arbitrary vector of real numbers (“logits”) into a valid probability distribution.

Definition 18.5 (Softmax Function) For any N real numbers \{v_i\}_{i \in [N]}, the softmax function gives us a probability distribution over [N] = \{1, \ldots, N\}: \text{Denote: } p = \text{Softmax}(\{v_i\}_{i \in [N]}) \in \mathbb{R}^N. \mathbb{P}(\text{random variable} = i) = p(i) = \frac{\exp(v_i)}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} \exp(v_j)}.
Equivalently, p(i) \propto \exp(v_i). Key insight: Softmax gives us a distribution.

The softmax function converts a vector of arbitrary real-valued scores (logits) into a valid probability distribution. The exponential function ensures all outputs are positive, and the normalization ensures they sum to one. Larger logits receive exponentially more probability mass, making softmax a “soft” version of the argmax operation.






TipRemark: Decoding (Unembedding) + Softmax



The TF produces a vector z_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^d. We can map z_\ell to \mathbb{R}^N, then apply softmax: \underbrace{W_U}_{\mathbb{R}^{N \times d}} \cdot z_\ell = \mathbb{R}^N \xrightarrow{\text{Softmax}} \text{distribution over } [N], \quad \text{e.g., over tokens with } N = V.
This is a softmax linear model.
Discriminative task: e.g., sentiment analysis — aggregate z_1, \ldots, z_L (e.g., z = \frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L} z_\ell), then feed into a softmax linear classifier: \mathbb{P}(\text{positive} \mid z) \propto \exp(w^\top z).
Autoregressive generation: use z_\ell to predict w_{\ell+1} via softmax linear classification.




18.4.2 Loss Function for Decoder-Only Model
With the softmax prediction head in place, we need a loss function to train the model. The natural choice for next-token prediction is to maximize the probability of the correct next token at each position, which leads to the cross-entropy loss. This is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation and is the standard training objective for all autoregressive language models.

Theorem 18.1 (Cross-Entropy Loss (Equivalent to MLE)) At each token position \ell \in [L], TF outputs z_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^d. After unembedding (W_U \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times V}) + softmax, we have a distribution p_\ell \in \Delta_L.
The next-token label is w_{\ell+1} (one-hot vector). The loss is: \text{Loss}(\theta) = -\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1} w_{\ell+1}^\top \log p_\ell = -\sum_{\ell=1}^{L-1} \log \mathbb{P}_\theta(w_{\ell+1} \mid w_1, \ldots, w_\ell).
This is the cross-entropy loss, equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Parameters \theta are trained via gradient-based optimization using backpropagation (see Part 2 for backpropagation and automatic differentiation).

The cross-entropy loss penalizes the model for assigning low probability to the correct next token. Minimizing this loss is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the training data, which connects transformer training directly to the statistical framework of maximum likelihood estimation studied throughout this course.


18.4.3 Token Embedding

Definition 18.6 (Word/Token Embedding) Each word w (a one-hot vector in \mathbb{R}^N) is associated with a vector x_w \in \mathbb{R}^d via an embedding matrix W_E \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times N}: x_i = W_E \, w_i \in \mathbb{R}^d.
The embedding matrix is learned from data. Input size: L \times N. Output size: L \times d.
For GPT-3: L = 2048, N = 50{,}257, d = 12{,}288.

The embedding matrix converts discrete tokens (represented as sparse one-hot vectors in a very high-dimensional space \mathbb{R}^N) into dense, continuous vectors in a much lower-dimensional space \mathbb{R}^d. This is essential because all subsequent operations in the transformer — attention, MLP layers, optimization — operate on continuous vectors.






TipRemark: Why Word Embedding?



Word embeddings equip words with “distance” to capture similarity. Using cosine similarity: \cos(u, v) = \frac{u^\top v}{\|u\| \cdot \|v\|}.
Similar words are close in the embedded space. Word2Vec and GloVe encode semantic meaning — interesting patterns emerge (e.g., king - man + woman \approx queen). Now we are in Euclidean space and it is easy to operate using calculus.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.5 4. Attention Mechanism
Attention treats each word’s representation as a query to access and incorporate information from a set of values.

Definition 18.7 (Attention) Given a set of vector values and a vector query, attention is a technique to compute a weighted sum of the values, dependent on the query. We say the query attends to the values.
Attention is just a weighted average — this is very powerful if the weights are learned!
In attention, the query matches all keys softly (weights between 0 and 1). In a lookup table, the query matches one key exactly.

The power of attention lies in its ability to dynamically route information: each token can selectively focus on the most relevant parts of the input, with the relevance weights learned from data. This is what allows transformers to capture long-range dependencies in sequences.

18.5.1 Cross Attention: The Equations
We now formalize the attention computation. The key idea is to use dot products between the query and each key to compute similarity scores, apply softmax to obtain weights, and then return the weighted sum of values. The 1/\sqrt{d_1} scaling factor prevents the dot products from growing too large in high dimensions, which would push softmax into regions of near-zero gradient.

Theorem 18.2 (Cross Attention Formula) Suppose we have (key, value) pairs \{(k_i, v_i)\}_{i \in [L]} with k_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1}, v_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}, and a query q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1}.

Compute similarity scores: e = (q^\top k_1, \ldots, q^\top k_L) \in \mathbb{R}^L
Similarity (attention weights): \alpha = \text{Softmax}(e) \in \Delta_L, where \alpha_i = \frac{\exp(k_i^\top q / \sqrt{d_1})}{\sum_{j=1}^{L} \exp(k_j^\top q / \sqrt{d_1})}. So \alpha_i = \mathbb{P}(k_i \text{ is closest to } q).
Aggregation: h = \sum_{i=1}^{L} \alpha_i \cdot v_i \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}

Output: (q, h) where q \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1}, h \in \mathbb{R}^{d'}.







TipRemark



Similarity is captured by k_i^\top q. The vector (k_1^\top q, \ldots, k_L^\top q) is called the attention score. We can use other functions in addition to softmax (e.g., ReLU).


An important structural property of the attention mechanism has a direct consequence for how we must handle sequential data.

Corollary 18.1 (Permutation Invariance) The attention output \sum_{i=1}^{L} \alpha_i \cdot v_i remains the same if we permute key-value pairs \{(k_i, v_i)\}_{i \in [L]}, because of the “\sum”.
Note: Ordering in a sequence matters. Natural language has order: “united states” \neq “states united”. We will address this with positional embeddings.

Permutation invariance is both a strength and a limitation. It means attention treats the input as a set rather than a sequence, which is why positional embeddings are essential for tasks where order matters, such as language modeling.


18.5.2 Self-Attention






Figure 18.1: Self-attention mechanism. The input sequence X is projected into queries Q, keys K, and values V via learned weight matrices. Attention weights are computed as \mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}), then applied to V to produce context-aware output representations.



Figure 18.1 illustrates the computation flow. The input matrix X \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d} is projected through three learned weight matrices to produce queries Q, keys K, and values V. Queries and keys are combined via the scaled dot product QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k} to form a raw attention-score matrix (one row per query token, one column per key token). The softmax normalizes each row into a probability distribution over positions, and the resulting attention weights are multiplied by V to produce the final output — a context-enriched representation where each token’s output is a weighted mixture of all value vectors.
In cross attention, the queries and key-value pairs come from different sources (e.g., the decoder queries the encoder). In a transformer’s main computation, however, each token in the sequence attends to all other tokens in the same sequence. This is called self-attention, and it is the mechanism that allows each token’s representation to incorporate contextual information from the entire input.

Definition 18.8 (Self-Attention) Self-attention is an attention module where query, key, value are all computed from the same input vectors. Given post-embedding sequence X = (x_1, \ldots, x_L) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}: Q = X W_Q, \quad K = X W_K, \quad V = X W_V \quad \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d_1},
where W_Q, W_K, W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_1} are learnable weight matrices.
For position \ell: \alpha_\ell = \text{Softmax}\!\left(\left\{q_\ell^\top k_j / \sqrt{d_1}\right\}_{j \in [L]}\right) \in \Delta_L.
The output at position \ell is: h_\ell = \sum_{j=1}^{L} \alpha_{\ell j} \cdot v_j = \sum_{j=1}^{L} \alpha_{\ell j} \cdot (W_V x_j).
Here \alpha_{\ell,j} measures the similarity between \{x_\ell, x_j\}: \alpha_{\ell j} = \frac{\exp(q_\ell^\top k_j / \sqrt{d_1})}{\sum_{s=1}^{L} \exp(q_\ell^\top k_s / \sqrt{d_1})} = \frac{\exp(x_\ell^\top W_Q^\top W_K x_j / \sqrt{d_1})}{\sum_{s=1}^{L} \exp(x_\ell^\top W_Q^\top W_K x_s / \sqrt{d_1})}.







ImportantAlgorithm: Self-Attention in Matrix Form



Input: X \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}, X = (x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_L).

Map into queries, keys, values: Q = X W_Q, K = X W_K, V = X W_V \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d_1}
Calculate attention score: E = Q K^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times L}
Apply softmax to each row: P = \text{Softmax}(E / \sqrt{d_1}) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times L}
Output = PV = \text{Softmax}(Q K^\top / \sqrt{d_1}) \cdot V



Figure 12.1: Attention weight matrix visualization. Each row shows how much each token attends to every other token. Brighter cells indicate stronger attention.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.6 5. Position Embedding
We want to include token position in the input. Since self-attention is permutation invariant, we need to explicitly encode order.

Definition 18.9 (Positional Embedding) A special trick of transformers: the embedding of (token, position) is additive: \text{emb}(\text{token}, \text{position}) = \text{emb}(\text{token}) + \text{emb}(\text{position}).
So x_i = \text{emb}(w_i) + \text{pe}_i \in \mathbb{R}^d, where d = dimension of word embedding.

The additive structure of positional embedding is a design choice that keeps the architecture simple: the model receives a single vector per token that encodes both what the token is and where it appears in the sequence. This allows the attention mechanism to use position information when computing relevance scores.
Three major practices of position embedding:

Absolute embedding: each \ell \mapsto \text{pe}_\ell, trained directly. Parameters: \{\text{pe}_1, \ldots, \text{pe}_L\} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d}.
Sinusoidal positional encoding (a special case of 3): use a fixed vector \vec{p}_t = \begin{pmatrix} \sin(\omega_1 \cdot t) \\ \cos(\omega_1 \cdot t) \\ \sin(\omega_2 \cdot t) \\ \cos(\omega_2 \cdot t) \\ \vdots \\ \sin(\omega_{d/2} \cdot t) \\ \cos(\omega_{d/2} \cdot t) \end{pmatrix}_{d \times 1}. This encodes relative positional information via rotation matrices.
Relative positional embedding: embed relative positions i - j. Map (i,j) \mapsto \vec{P}_{i-j} with learnable vectors. Used in RoPE (Rotary Position Embedding, used in LLaMA). The attention score formula becomes: \alpha_i = \text{Softmax}\!\left(\{q_i^\top(k_j + \vec{P}_{i-j})\}_{j \in [L]}\right).

Figure 12.2: Sinusoidal positional encoding heatmap. Each row is a position, each column a dimension of the encoding vector. Low-frequency sinusoids vary slowly across positions while high-frequency ones oscillate rapidly.

title: 18  Transformers
section: 18.7 6. Causal Masking: Don’t See the Future
text:
18.7 6. Causal Masking: Don’t See the Future
For autoregressive generation, the model must predict token w_{\ell+1} using only w_1, \ldots, w_\ell. But standard self-attention lets every token attend to every other token, including future ones. Causal masking enforces the autoregressive constraint by preventing information from flowing backward in time.

Definition 18.10 (Causal Masking) In decoder-only models, we need to ensure that token \ell cannot attend to future tokens. We manually set \alpha_{\ell j} = 0 for all j > \ell.
To achieve this:

If j > \ell: set \text{Mask}_{\ell j} = -\infty
If j \leq \ell: set \text{Mask}_{\ell j} = 0

\text{Attention score} = \text{Softmax}(Q K^\top + \text{Mask}).
After softmax, the -\infty elements become zero.
Note: Only use causal masking for decoder TF. Encoder-only models (like BERT) use full (global) attention.

Causal masking enforces the autoregressive property at the architectural level: by preventing each token from attending to future positions, we ensure that the prediction of w_{\ell+1} depends only on w_1, \ldots, w_\ell. This is what makes left-to-right text generation possible during inference.
Figure 12.3: Left — Global (encoder) attention mask: all tokens attend to all tokens. Right — Causal (decoder) attention mask: each token only attends to itself and previous tokens.

title: 18  Transformers
section: 18.8 7. Add MLP Layers After Each Attention Layer
text:
18.8 7. Add MLP Layers After Each Attention Layer
Self-attention output \sum_{j=1}^{L} \alpha_{\ell j} \cdot W_V x_j is a weighted average of linear functions of embeddings. We need to add nonlinearities.

Definition 18.11 (MLP / Feed-Forward Layer) The MLP is a 2-layer neural network applied independently for each position \ell \in [L]: m_\ell = \text{MLP}(\text{output}_\ell) : \mathbb{R}^{d_1} \to \mathbb{R}^{d_1} = W_2 \cdot \sigma(W_1 x + b_1) + b_2,
where \sigma is a nonlinearity (ReLU or GELU), W_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1 \times d_f}, b_1 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_f}, W_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_f \times d_1}, b_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1}.
Typically d_f \gg d_1. In GPT-3: d_f = 4d.
The same MLP is applied independently for each \ell \in [L].

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.9 8. Multi-Head Attention
Instead of having a single attention module, we use multi-head self attention: multiple (H) attention heads in parallel.

Definition 18.12 (Multi-Head Attention) H = number of attention heads. Each head has three matrices \{W_K^h, W_Q^h, W_V^h\}_{h \in [H]}, each \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_1}, where d_1 = d / H.
At each position \ell, input x_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^d, d = H \cdot d_1:

Head h looks at x_\ell^{(h)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d_1} (the h-th chunk of the vector)
\text{Output}^h = \sum_{j=1}^{L} \alpha_{\ell j}^h \cdot v_j^h for each head h
Final output = W_O \begin{pmatrix} \text{output}^1 \\ \text{output}^2 \\ \vdots \\ \text{output}^H \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^d, where W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} is the output matrix that mixes across heads.








TipRemark: Each Head Captures Different Semantics



Different attention heads learn to attend to different patterns: some heads focus on adjacent tokens, some on syntactic relationships, some on semantic similarity. This is visible when visualizing attention matrices from different heads.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.10 9. Residual Connections & Layer Normalization
A transformer decoder stacks dozens (or even nearly a hundred) layers of attention and MLP blocks. Training such deep networks without any architectural tricks would be nearly impossible due to vanishing or exploding gradients. Two key ingredients make deep transformers trainable: residual connections and layer normalization.

Definition 18.13 (Residual Connection) Instead of X^{(i)} = \text{Layer}(X^{(i-1)}), we let: X^{(i)} = X^{(i-1)} + \text{Layer}(X^{(i-1)}).
That is: X \mapsto X + \text{MHA}(X). Add the input to the output of multi-head attention. This biases the mapping to identity, so we only have to learn “the residual.”

Residual connections are critical for training deep networks: they provide a direct gradient pathway from the output back to earlier layers, preventing the vanishing gradient problem. From an optimization perspective, they make the loss landscape smoother and easier to navigate.
Layer normalization complements residual connections by stabilizing the distribution of activations across layers. Without normalization, the scale of hidden representations can drift unpredictably as data passes through many layers, making optimization difficult.

Definition 18.14 (Layer Normalization) Normalization applied to each feature vector individually. For a vector x \in \mathbb{R}^d:

Mean: \mu = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^{d} x_j
Standard deviation: \sigma = \sqrt{\frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^{d} (x_j - \mu)^2}
Normalization: v = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma + \varepsilon}, where \varepsilon is a small number to avoid numerical instability

Do this operation LayerNorm: x \mapsto v for all x in the sequence: x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_L \in \mathbb{R}^d.

Layer normalization stabilizes training by ensuring that the inputs to each sub-layer have consistent scale, regardless of the activations from previous layers. This is particularly important in deep transformers with many stacked blocks, where without normalization the magnitude of activations can grow or shrink uncontrollably.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.11 10. Full Transformer Architecture






The Transformer Decoder is a stack of Transformer Decoder Blocks. Each Block consists of:

(Masked) Multi-Head Self-Attention
Add & Norm (residual connection + layer norm)
Feed-Forward Network (MLP)
Add & Norm

Two design choices: Post-norm (original): LN after each sub-layer. Pre-norm (more popular now): LN before each sub-layer, for better training stability.









TipRemark: Revisiting Model Types




Encoder-only: Do not use causal masking. In training, hide (mask) some random tokens and predict them. Example: BERT.
Decoder-only: Use causal masking to mask the future. Trained to predict next token. Example: GPT.
Encoder-Decoder: Output of encoder is fed into decoder blocks, attended by features of decoder using cross attention (at each layer). Example: T5.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.12 Exercise: Understanding GPT-3 Parameters
GPT-3 175B: n_\text{layers} = 96, d_\text{model} = 12288, n_\text{heads} = 96, d_\text{head} = 128. Context window L = 2048, vocabulary size N = 50257. Note: d = H \times d_1.






ImportantAlgorithm: Computing the Number of Parameters




Word embedding: W_E \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times d} \Rightarrow \#\text{param} = N \cdot d
Position embedding: W_{PE} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d} \Rightarrow \#\text{param} = L \cdot d
Each self-attention layer: Each W_Q^h, W_K^h, W_V^h \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d_1} \Rightarrow \#\text{param} = 3 \times d \times d_1 \times H = 3d^2. Output matrix W_O \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d} \Rightarrow d^2. Total MHA: 4d^2 per layer \times n_\text{layer}.
MLP layer: (W_1, W_2, b_1, b_2) \Rightarrow \approx 4d \times d \times 2 = 8d^2 per layer \times n_\text{layer}.

Neglecting biases and layer norms: \#\text{param} = N \cdot d + L \cdot d + 12 \cdot d^2 \times n_\text{layer} \approx 174{,}074{,}267{,}648 \approx 174 \times 10^9 \quad (99.5\% \text{ accurate}).

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.13 Transformer Circuits & Residual Stream
We can view a Transformer as a model that processes a sequence of tokens in multiple layers. In each layer, the vector at the same position is processed by attention, normalization, and MLP. The vector itself is added directly to the next layer by residual connection.

Theorem 18.3 (Single-Layer Attention-Only Transformer) For a single-layer attention-only transformer:

Token embedding: x_0 = W_E \, t, where t = \binom{w}{i} \in \mathbb{R}^{L+V} (token + position)
Attention: x_1 = x_0 + \sum_{h \in H} h(x_0)
Logits: T(t) = W_U x_{-1} (unembedding)

Define the QK-matrix: W_{QK}^h = (W_Q^h)^\top W_K^h / \sqrt{d} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}
and the OV-matrix: W_{OV}^h = W_O^h W_V^h \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}.
Then: A^h = \text{Softmax}(X_0 \, W_{QK}^h \, X_0^\top) \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times L}, and we can write the full model as: T(x) = X \underbrace{(W_U W_E)^\top}_{\text{residual}} + \sum_{h=1}^{H} A^h \cdot X \cdot \underbrace{(W_U W_{OV}^h W_E)}_{\text{a single matrix}}.
where X is the input sequence, A^h = \text{Softmax}(X \, W_{QK}^h \, X^\top).

title: 18  Transformers
text:
18.14 Interactive Demos
The following code computes attention weights for a simple self-attention example. Edit and run to explore.

18.14.1 Self-Attention Computation
#| eval: false
import numpy as np

# Simple self-attention example
np.random.seed(42)
L = 4  # sequence length
d = 8  # embedding dimension
d1 = 4  # attention head dimension

# Simulated token embeddings (e.g., "I", "love", "deep", "learning")
tokens = ["I", "love", "deep", "learning"]
X = np.random.randn(L, d)

# Weight matrices
W_Q = np.random.randn(d, d1) * 0.3
W_K = np.random.randn(d, d1) * 0.3
W_V = np.random.randn(d, d1) * 0.3

# Compute Q, K, V
Q = X @ W_Q  # (L, d1)
K = X @ W_K
V = X @ W_V

# Attention scores
E = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d1)  # (L, L)
print("Raw attention scores (Q K^T / sqrt(d1)):")
print(np.round(E, 3))

# Softmax (row-wise)
def softmax(x):
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True)

alpha = softmax(E)
print("\nAttention weights (after softmax):")
for i, tok in enumerate(tokens):
    weights = ", ".join(f"{tokens[j]}: {alpha[i,j]:.3f}" for j in range(L))
    print(f"  {tok} attends to -> {weights}")

# Output
output = alpha @ V
print(f"\nOutput shape: {output.shape}")
print(f"Output (first 3 dims):\n{np.round(output[:, :3], 3)}")

# Causal mask for decoder
print("\n--- With Causal Masking ---")
mask = np.triu(np.ones((L, L)) * (-1e9), k=1)
E_masked = E + mask
alpha_causal = softmax(E_masked)
print("Causal attention weights:")
for i, tok in enumerate(tokens):
    weights = ", ".join(f"{tokens[j]}: {alpha_causal[i,j]:.3f}" for j in range(L))
    print(f"  {tok} attends to -> {weights}")


18.14.2 GPT-3 Parameter Count
#| eval: false
import numpy as np

# GPT-3 175B configuration
configs = {
    "GPT-3 Small":  {"n_params_official": "125M",  "n_layers": 12, "d_model": 768,   "n_heads": 12, "d_head": 64},
    "GPT-3 Medium": {"n_params_official": "350M",  "n_layers": 24, "d_model": 1024,  "n_heads": 16, "d_head": 64},
    "GPT-3 Large":  {"n_params_official": "760M",  "n_layers": 24, "d_model": 1536,  "n_heads": 16, "d_head": 96},
    "GPT-3 XL":     {"n_params_official": "1.3B",  "n_layers": 24, "d_model": 2048,  "n_heads": 24, "d_head": 128},
    "GPT-3 175B":   {"n_params_official": "175.0B","n_layers": 96, "d_model": 12288, "n_heads": 96, "d_head": 128},
}

N = 50257  # vocabulary size
L = 2048   # context window

print(f"Vocabulary size N = {N}")
print(f"Context window  L = {L}")
print(f"{'Model':<16} {'Official':>10} {'Computed':>16} {'Accuracy':>10}")
print("-" * 56)

for name, cfg in configs.items():
    d = cfg["d_model"]
    n_layer = cfg["n_layers"]

    # 1. Word embedding: N * d
    word_emb = N * d
    # 2. Position embedding: L * d
    pos_emb = L * d
    # 3. Self-attention: 4*d^2 per layer
    attn = 4 * d**2 * n_layer
    # 4. MLP: 8*d^2 per layer
    mlp = 8 * d**2 * n_layer

    total = word_emb + pos_emb + attn + mlp

    # Parse official
    official_str = cfg["n_params_official"]
    if "B" in official_str:
        official = float(official_str.replace("B","")) * 1e9
    else:
        official = float(official_str.replace("M","")) * 1e6

    accuracy = total / official * 100
    print(f"{name:<16} {official_str:>10} {total:>16,} {accuracy:>9.1f}%")
Figure 12.4: Dot product of sinusoidal positional encodings across positions. The diagonal structure shows that nearby positions have similar encodings, encoding relative position information.






TipRemark: Looking Ahead



This concludes the course. The optimization foundations developed throughout—from convexity and duality to first-order methods and stochastic optimization—provide the mathematical toolkit for understanding and advancing modern machine learning.

title: 18  Transformers
text:
Summary

Attention mechanism. The core operation computes \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\bigl(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\bigr)V, where queries, keys, and values are linear projections of the input; this allows each token to attend to all other tokens with learned, content-dependent weights.
Positional encoding. Since self-attention is permutation-equivariant, sinusoidal positional encodings \operatorname{PE}(pos, 2i) = \sin(pos / 10000^{2i/d}) inject sequence-order information; causal masking further enforces autoregressive structure by preventing attention to future tokens.
Transformer block. Each block applies multi-head self-attention followed by a position-wise MLP, with residual connections and layer normalization (x + \operatorname{Sublayer}(x)) around each sub-layer—enabling stable training of very deep models.
Multi-head attention. Running h attention heads in parallel with independent projections W_i^Q, W_i^K, W_i^V lets the model capture diverse relational patterns; outputs are concatenated and linearly projected back to the model dimension.

title: Course Summary
text:
Preparation
This course has taken you on a journey through the core of mathematical optimization — from the foundational theory of convexity that tells us what an optimal solution looks like, through the first- and second-order algorithms that find one, to the classical theory of linear programming and the modern constrained optimization methods that power industrial solvers. Along the way, we saw how these ideas come alive in two of the most consequential applications of our time: diffusion models and transformers. The unifying theme throughout has been the interplay between structure and algorithms: convexity, smoothness, strong convexity, and constraint geometry each unlock specific algorithmic strategies with provable guarantees.
We began with the observation that optimization problems arise everywhere — in maximum likelihood estimation, regression, portfolio optimization, and neural network training — and that the common thread running through the tractable cases is convexity. We built the mathematical toolkit needed to recognize and exploit convex structure: norms and inner products, eigenvalues and spectral decompositions, gradients, Hessians, Taylor expansions, and the chain rule for backpropagation.

title: Course Summary
text:
Convex Optimization Basics
With the mathematical foundations in hand, we developed the theory of convex sets (polyhedra, cones, ellipsoids), convex functions (first- and second-order characterizations, operations preserving convexity), and the key consequence that every local minimum of a convex function is a global minimum. We then developed the theory of Lagrangian duality, which associates every constrained optimization problem with a dual problem whose optimal value bounds the original. Under Slater’s constraint qualification, this bound is tight (strong duality holds), and the KKT conditions provide a complete characterization of optimality. The hierarchy of convex programs — LP, QP, SOCP, SDP — gave us a taxonomy of increasingly expressive problem classes, each solvable by specialized algorithms.

title: Course Summary
text:
First-Order Methods
With the theoretical foundations in place, we turned to algorithms. Gradient descent — the simplest and most fundamental iterative method — follows the negative gradient to reduce the objective at each step. We proved convergence rates under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions and saw how the condition number \kappa = M/m governs the speed of convergence. Momentum methods (Polyak’s heavy ball, Nesterov’s accelerated gradient) reduce the dependence on \kappa from linear to a square root, while adaptive methods (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam) automatically scale the step size per coordinate. Stochastic gradient descent made large-scale training feasible by replacing the full gradient with a cheap, noisy estimate, and proximal gradient methods extended first-order optimization to composite objectives with nonsmooth regularizers like the \ell_1 norm. For constrained problems, projected subgradient descent handles nonsmooth objectives over convex sets, while the Frank-Wolfe (conditional gradient) method offers a projection-free alternative when linear minimization is cheap.

title: Course Summary
text:
Linear Programming
Linear programming occupies a central place in optimization, both for its theoretical elegance and its enormous practical reach. We developed the geometry of LP — vertices, edges, and faces of polyhedra — and showed that every LP with a finite optimum has an optimal vertex. The transition to equational form and basic feasible solutions gave us the algebraic machinery behind the simplex method, which moves from vertex to vertex along improving edges. Despite its exponential worst-case complexity (the Klee–Minty cube), the simplex method is extraordinarily efficient in practice. LP duality provided a parallel problem whose optimal value matches the primal’s, and the dual simplex method exploits this structure for sensitivity analysis and warm-starting. We applied LP to network flow problems (max-flow/min-cut), and extended the framework to robust optimization and game theory, where LP duality yields the minimax theorem.

title: Course Summary
text:
Second-Order and Interior Point Methods
Newton’s method incorporates curvature information through the Hessian, achieving quadratic convergence near the optimum at the cost of solving a linear system at each iteration. Its affine invariance means it is immune to the ill-conditioning that plagues gradient descent. Modern matrix optimizers — Muon, Shampoo, and SOAP — extend these preconditioning ideas to the matrix geometry of neural network weight parameters through spectral norms, SVD-based updates, and Kronecker-factored preconditioners. The ellipsoid method resolved one of the great open questions in optimization by proving that LP can be solved in polynomial time: it maintains an ellipsoid guaranteed to contain the optimum, halving its volume at each step via a separating hyperplane. Finally, interior point methods extend Newton’s method to inequality-constrained problems through a logarithmic barrier, following the central path as the barrier parameter decreases. These methods achieve polynomial complexity and practical efficiency, and they are the engine behind modern solvers like MOSEK, Gurobi, and CVXPY.

title: Course Summary
text:
Modern Computation Models
We concluded with two applications that illustrate how optimization underpins frontier AI systems. Diffusion models learn to generate photorealistic images by training a neural network to reverse a noise-corruption process — the training objective reduces to a regression problem solved by SGD and backpropagation. Transformers, the architecture behind GPT, Claude, and LLaMA, are built from matrix multiplications, softmax operations, and the attention mechanism, all trained end-to-end with the gradient-based methods developed throughout the course. These chapters demonstrated that the “abstract” optimization theory from earlier in the course is precisely what powers the most impactful AI systems today.

title: Course Summary
text:
Where to Go Next
This course has given you the practical optimization toolkit: you can formulate problems as convex programs, select an appropriate algorithm, and predict its convergence behavior. But there is much more to the story. S&DS 432/632: Advanced Optimization Techniques develops the theoretical depth and modern research connections that build on everything covered here.
In the advanced course, you will study duality theory in far greater depth — not just as a tool for optimality conditions, but as a design principle for algorithms. Mirror descent generalizes projected gradient descent by replacing the Euclidean geometry with a Bregman divergence tailored to the problem structure, yielding optimal algorithms for simplex-constrained and entropy-regularized problems. You will see accelerated methods derived from first principles, paired with information-theoretic lower bounds that prove these rates cannot be improved — settling the question of what is fundamentally achievable in first-order optimization. The course also explores implicit layers, which embed optimization problems as differentiable layers inside neural networks, enabling end-to-end learning of systems that solve optimization at inference time.
In short, this course gave you the algorithms and the intuition; the advanced course reveals why they work, when they are optimal, and how to push beyond their limits. The transition from practitioner to researcher begins there.
